zh_summary: Patrick Moorhead：許多 NVIDIA 供應協議是與 Jensen 的握手而非書面合約的說法只對了一半。Jensen 確實在房間裡做出重大決定。一些 NVIDIA 最大客戶的 CEO 告訴我本週有十億美元級承諾當場做出。最大交易的風險被誇大了，因為它們是書面的。NVIDIA 披露截至七月有 2790 億美元供應和產能承諾，較前一季 1190 億美元上升，由記憶體驅動。其中 2670 億美元安排至財政 2029 年。NVIDIA 在 2025 年成為台積電最大客戶。兩大 HBM 供應商正在收緊合約，使買家無法退出。供應和路線圖至少在 18 個月內大多已設定。真正的風險是下一輪未書面的部分，以及 NVIDIA 是否繼續以 Jensen 的步伐承諾。對手將競標它所不承諾的。Colette Kress 一直在電話中安撫供應商。週二的 $NVDA 電話是她作為臨時 CEO 的第一次，她將展示現在誰做重大決定。
text:
The take that many NVIDIA supply deals were "a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract" is half right.

Jensen did made the big calls in the room. CEOs of some of NVIDIA's largest customers told me that this past week. Billion-dollar commitments, made on the spot. I'd bet suppliers saw the same. That is hard to replace.

What's overstated is the risk to the biggest deals. They're on paper.

• NVIDIA disclosed $279B in supply and capacity commitments as of July, up from $119B a quarter earlier, driven by memory. $267B of it is scheduled through fiscal 2029. You can’t report it without more than a handshake. 
• NVIDIA became TSMC's largest customer in 2025. The two biggest HBM suppliers are tightening contracts so buyers can't back out. Suppliers aren't the flight risk.
• I've said supply and the roadmap are mostly set for at least 18 months.

The real exposure is the next round: anything not on paper, and whether NVIDIA keeps committing at Jensen's pace. Rivals will bid for whatever it doesn't.

NVIDIA has a deep bench, and Colette Kress has been on calls reassuring suppliers. Tuesday's $NVDA call, her first as interim CEO, is where she shows who makes the big calls now.

Compute pricing is becoming as much about contract duration as the chips themselves with 5-year deals across $IREN and $CRWV around $20–25 per watt-year versus $40–50 for short-term capacity and new $SPCX contracts above $50.

That spread creates an interesting opportunity for $NBIS whose 2026 base sits near $12 while newer short-term deals exceed $40 leaving room for realized pricing to rise as its contract mix shifts toward higher rates.

You can see the same dynamic within SpaceX where $ANT initial agreement priced near $30 while $GOOGL is paying $53–79 including H100s at more than 3x the rental index suggesting contract timing and guaranteed access are becoming just as important as the GPU itself.

text:
Ok I thought about this a bit more. It took me a while to finally understand what @dwarkesh_sp was getting at by casting the discussion into a formal economics model. We were simply talking past each other.

Fundamentally, the “intuition” Dwarkesh was pointing to is that AI research progress is produced by a combination of researcher effort and experiment compute that are imperfect substitutes. The production function of AI capability is concave (“isoquants” are convex), so using a more balanced mix is always more productive for a given budget than being stuck in a corner.

Research automation changes this in two distinct ways. First, it raises the effective quantity of the researcher input since automated researchers work much faster and continuously, so each one delivers say “50×” more researcher input per calendar week. Because of concavity, that does not translate into a 50× speedup in final research output for a fixed compute budget; Dwarkesh’s rough lower bound is still something like “5×”.

Second, and perhaps more importantly, automation also raises the productivity of the AI capability production process itself. It’s almost like there’s a technology or productivity multiplier that rises with each generation of smarter models. Once models match the best humans, every automated researcher is at the level of today’s top researchers (in his words), and the work is modular enough to be highly parallelized. I have been obsessed with learning about business and investing since I was a young kid. I would voraciously read books and articles about the world’s most successful founders, executives, and investors. I wanted to understand how they built their fortunes and I was motivated by their stories.

Author @JackCarrUSA highlighted a pattern I kept noticing: Even a pawn can take down a king.

It is no secret that wealthy, powerful people are in constant competition with each other. They are trying to find asymmetric opportunities and exploit them for their own gain. Business is a giant game of risk-taking played by some of the smartest, most ruthless people in the world.

THE HARDEST TAPE IN YEARS. 

This is not the worst market, but arguably the hardest one to win in. $NBIS can rally double digits one day and give it all back over the next two. $SPY and $QQQ reclaim key levels only to lose them again. The AI story hasn’t disappeared, but the market has moved from asking who benefits from AI to who ultimately pays for it. Capex, debt, funding and cash flow now matter as much as demand. In this environment, being right about the company, the earnings, or even the macro isn’t enough if the market disagrees with your timing. You can get four out of five things right and still lose money. That’s why this is a market for discipline, patience and proper position sizing, not oversized conviction. Know what you own, know why you own it, keep cash available, and don’t let short-term volatility force long-term decisions. Easy markets make everyone look like a genius. Difficult markets reveal who actually has a process. The edge right now isn’t predicting every move. It’s surviving the uncertainty long enough for your thesis to play out.
